content.content:
## Walkthrough Notes
Why doesn't a failed insert corrupt the tree?
Both fallible allocations happen before the first tree pointer is changed.

What happens if node allocation succeeds but key allocation fails?
The unlinked node is freed and -1 is returned; the caller still owns the value.

Why don't overwrite and delete need allocation-failure handling?
They allocate nothing.

Why must the sweep eventually terminate?
The fixed scenario performs finitely many allocations, so eventually n is larger than all of them.

## Notes/Tips from Spec
Mutation 3 asks for a tree of a million
nodes, and valgrind runs many times slower than native. Put the million-node case behind a flag
or its own target so make memcheck still finishes inside a coffee break: run the large case under
asan, which is fast enough, and a smaller case under valgrind. What you must not do is quietly
shrink the large case because a timing problem was inconvenient. If your harness ends up running
the “million-node” teardown at ten thousand nodes, say so in REFLECTION.md, and expect the
walkthrough to ask about it.

## Thresholds
4096-byte slabs. O(1)
for pool_alloc and
pool_free. 106 nodes
under a 64 KB stack. live
+ free_objs == slabs *
objs_per_slab. Zero leaks,
not few.
## Choices left up to me
Where the slab header lives.
What alignment you guarantee and how the stride enforces it. Right-spine teardown or pointer reversal? Morris or parent pointers? What
your rb_foreach contract 
says about callbacks that call
back in?
DECIDED (2026-10-06, Mutation 2 pool design — recorded before any `src/pool.c` code exists):

**1. Alignment.** Slots are aligned to `_Alignof(max_align_t)` (fundamental alignment). The
slot stride is `obj_size` rounded up to that alignment, and is also never smaller than
`sizeof(void *)` so a dead slot can hold the intrusive free-list `next`. Because the first
slot's offset inside the slab and the stride are both multiples of that alignment, and the
block `rb_malloc` returns is already `max_align_t`-aligned, *every* slot address
(`base + start + i*stride`) is aligned — not just slot 0. Getting only slot 0 right is the
version of this bug that works and then works less.

Why: `pool_create(size_t obj_size)` takes no alignment parameter, so the pool cannot be told
what its caller needs and has to promise one unilaterally. The conservative fundamental
promise costs some internal padding when `obj_size` is not already a multiple of it — for the
current ~48-byte `struct rb_node` that cost happens to be zero, which is an accident worth
noticing and not relying on — and buys a guarantee that stays true if the node layout changes.
It also satisfies both uses a slot's bytes are put to across its lifetime: the live object
while it is live, and the free-list pointer written over its front when it dies. The spec
flags this as a `-fsanitize=undefined` matter ("alignment is one of those requirements that
feels ceremonial until it is wrong"), and `make asan` is a gate, so a misalignment here is a
build failure rather than a mystery.

LIMIT (explicit): `max_align_t` is a *fundamental*-alignment guarantee only. It is not support
for over-aligned types — anything demanding more than `max_align_t` via `_Alignas` (a
cache-line-aligned or over-aligned SIMD object, say) is outside this pool's contract and would
need an alignment parameter the frozen API does not have.

**2. Slab metadata: in-band**, at the front of each 4096-byte slab.

Why: one `rb_malloc` per slab, and therefore exactly one failure point when the pool grows.
Out-of-band metadata would add a second allocation per slab, which means a second failure path
with a real unwind (slab bought, header allocation fails => release the slab and leave the
pool's counters untouched) and a second object for `pool_destroy` to release. In-band trades
payload space to keep the pool's only failure mode "buy a new slab."

Cost accepted: usable space is `4096 - header - alignment padding`, not 4096, so
`objs_per_slab` must be derived from what is left after the header. That is precisely the
off-by-one Figure 4's caption warns about ("the slab header, which eats bytes the naive
division forgets") and that the spec's own adversarial-review prompt for M2 tells the reviewer
to hunt for, alongside the tail slack that must never be handed out.

Consequence for teardown: the next-slab link lives *inside* the block being released, so
`pool_destroy` must read `next` before `rb_free`ing that slab — the same "save the pointer
before you free the thing that contains it" rule as the HW1 right-spine teardown, one level
down.

Not relied on: the spec notes that in-band metadata makes "which slab is this object in?"
answerable by masking. That requires page-*aligned* slabs, and `rb_malloc` forwards to
`malloc`, which guarantees `max_align_t` (16 bytes), not 4096 — so masking is not actually
available here and forms no part of this justification. Nothing in this design needs the
object->slab mapping anyway: a single intrusive free list makes `pool_free` indifferent to
which slab an object came from, which is what keeps it O(1).

**3. `pool_stats` / `free_objs`:** the spec's operational definition — every slot that already
exists which `pool_alloc` could return without calling `rb_malloc` again. That is free-list
slots **plus** uncarved capacity in slabs already bought, because `pool_alloc` satisfies both
without allocating and the caller cannot tell which path a slot arrived by. Hence
`live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`.

What that invariant actually asserts: every slot that exists is in exactly one of three states
— live, on the free list, or never yet carved — with the last two both counting as
`free_objs`, and none lost or double-counted. Tail slack is not a slot and contributes to
neither side. It therefore catches a slot dropped on the floor, a slot handed out twice, a
double `pool_free` (which also makes the free list cyclic), a carve loop that steps one slot
into the slack, and a slab counted before its allocation actually succeeded — including after
an injected failure, when it must still hold. Per the spec it is asserted repeatedly while the
allocator is under stress, not once at the end: "the earliest assertion failure is usually much
more informative than the corpse you discover ten thousand operations later."

Still open (deliberately not decided yet): whether the three numbers come from maintained
counters, an on-demand walk of the free list, or counters plus a debug-only walk that
cross-checks them; how the tests get at `objs_per_slab`, given the public API does not expose
it and having the tests recompute it would let a geometry bug cancel out of its own check;
whether `pool_stats` tolerates NULL out-parameters; whether `pool_create` buys a slab eagerly
or lazily; and what a `obj_size` too large to fit even once should do.


## Confusions
“Why does pool reuse hide useafter-free from ASan?” “What
exactly happens between the
node alloc and the key copy?”
“Why can’t the teardown loop
spin forever?”

while it is live, and the free-list pointer written over its front when it dies. The spec
flags this as a `-fsanitize=undefined` matter ("alignment is one of those requirements that
feels ceremonial until it is wrong"), and `make asan` is a gate, so a misalignment here is a
build failure rather than a mystery.

LIMIT (explicit): `max_align_t` is a *fundamental*-alignment guarantee only. It is not support
for over-aligned types — anything demanding more than `max_align_t` via `_Alignas` (a
cache-line-aligned or over-aligned SIMD object, say) is outside this pool's contract and would
need an alignment parameter the frozen API does not have.

**2. Slab metadata: in-band**, at the front of each 4096-byte slab.

Why: one `rb_malloc` per slab, and therefore exactly one failure point when the pool grows.
Out-of-band metadata would add a second allocation per slab, which means a second failure path
with a real unwind (slab bought, header allocation fails => release the slab and leave the
pool's counters untouched) and a second object for `pool_destroy` to release. In-band trades
payload space to keep the pool's only failure mode "buy a new slab."

Cost accepted: usable space is `4096 - header - alignment padding`, not 4096, so
`objs_per_slab` must be derived from what is left after the header. That is precisely the
off-by-one Figure 4's caption warns about ("the slab header, which eats bytes the naive
division forgets") and that the spec's own adversarial-review prompt for M2 tells the reviewer
to hunt for, alongside the tail slack that must never be handed out.

Consequence for teardown: the next-slab link lives *inside* the block being released, so
`pool_destroy` must read `next` before `rb_free`ing that slab — the same "save the pointer
before you free the thing that contains it" rule as the HW1 right-spine teardown, one level
down.

Not relied on: the spec notes that in-band metadata makes "which slab is this object in?"
answerable by masking. That requires page-*aligned* slabs, and `rb_malloc` forwards to
`malloc`, which guarantees `max_align_t` (16 bytes), not 4096 — so masking is not actually
available here and forms no part of this justification. Nothing in this design needs the
object->slab mapping anyway: a single intrusive free list makes `pool_free` indifferent to
which slab an object came from, which is what keeps it O(1).

**3. `pool_stats` / `free_objs`:** the spec's operational definition — every slot that already
exists which `pool_alloc` could return without calling `rb_malloc` again. That is free-list
slots **plus** uncarved capacity in slabs already bought, because `pool_alloc` satisfies both
without allocating and the caller cannot tell which path a slot arrived by. Hence
`live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`.

What that invariant actually asserts: every slot that exists is in exactly one of three states
— live, on the free list, or never yet carved — with the last two both counting as
`free_objs`, and none lost or double-counted. Tail slack is not a slot and contributes to
neither side. It therefore catches a slot dropped on the floor, a slot handed out twice, a
double `pool_free` (which also makes the free list cyclic), a carve loop that steps one slot
into the slack, and a slab counted before its allocation actually succeeded — including after
an injected failure, when it must still hold. Per the spec it is asserted repeatedly while the
allocator is under stress, not once at the end: "the earliest assertion failure is usually much
more informative than the corpse you discover ten thousand operations later."

Still open (deliberately not decided yet): whether the three numbers come from maintained
counters, an on-demand walk of the free list, or counters plus a debug-only walk that
cross-checks them; how the tests get at `objs_per_slab`, given the public API does not expose
it and having the tests recompute it would let a geometry bug cancel out of its own check;
whether `pool_stats` tolerates NULL out-parameters; whether `pool_create` buys a slab eagerly
or lazily; and what a `obj_size` too large to fit even once should do.


## Confusions
“Why does pool reuse hide useafter-free from ASan?” “What
exactly happens between the
node alloc and the key copy?”
“Why can’t the teardown loop
spin forever?”

content.text:
Inspected: `src/pool.c` (geometry only, `rb_pool_geometry` + in-band `struct rb_slab`), `tests/test_rbtree.c` (the `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` extern-declaration precedent and the hand-literal geometry table), `Makefile` (`src/pool.c` already in `SRC`; `-DRBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` only on the unit binary), `tests/fault_alloc.h` (`arm`/`disarm`/`total`), NOTES.md §"Choices left up to me" (decisions 1–3 + the "Still open" list), DEVLOG 2026-10-06/07.

No edits made. Proposal below.

---

## 0. One framing note first

The pool is a **client** of the `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` seam tonight, not a replacement for it. Slabs come from `rb_malloc`, which is exactly what makes every fault-injection test below possible. Only on Evening 6 does the pool sit *between* the tree and the seam. Nothing tonight should assume otherwise.

Second: `src/pool.c` has no header by design (NOTES.md decision). Tests reach the pool the same way they reach `rb_pool_geometry` — declaring it themselves under `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`. `rb_pool_t` stays **incomplete** to the test: the test declares `typedef struct rb_pool rb_pool_t;` and the five prototypes, and never sees the layout. That's strictly better than the geometry case, because there is no struct to duplicate and therefore no layout to drift.

---

## 1. `rb_pool_t` fields

Five groups. Geometry is computed **once** in `pool_create` and cached, so `pool_alloc`/`pool_free` never divide or round — that is what makes O(1) real rather than nominal, and it means `rb_pool_geometry`'s return value is checked at exactly one place in the program.

**Geometry (frozen at create, read-only after):**
- `obj_size` — what the caller asked for. Kept for `pool_stats`/diagnostics and so a later `rb_create_pooled` can assert it against `sizeof(struct rb_node)`.
- `stride` — bytes per slot.
- `slot0_offset` — first slot's offset from slab base.
- `objs_per_slab` — the right-hand side of the headline invariant. Must be stored, not recomputed, or the invariant check re-derives one of its own operands.
- (`slack` is deliberately **not** stored. It is an output of the geometry helper that exists to be asserted in the geometry test; the pool never needs it, because "is there room for another slot" is answered by `carve_remaining`, not by arithmetic against the slab end. Storing it would invite a second, redundant way to decide the same thing.)

**Slab chain:**
- `struct rb_slab *slabs` — head of the singly-linked in-band chain, newest first (LIFO push on grow). Exists solely so `pool_destroy` can walk it; nothing on the hot path reads it.

**Carve state:**
- `unsigned char *carve_next` — address of the next never-yet-carved slot, always inside the **head** slab.
- `size_t carve_remaining` — uncarved slots left in the head slab.

One cursor pair suffices because of an invariant worth writing as a comment in the file: *every slab except the head is fully carved.* That holds because growth only happens when `carve_remaining == 0`. If growth were ever allowed earlier, the old head's uncarved slots would become unreachable — `free_objs` slots that `pool_alloc` can never return — which breaks the headline invariant's real meaning ("no slot lost on the floor"). So this field choice and decision 4 below are the same decision.

A detail to get right at implementation time: after carving the last slot, advancing `carve_next` by `stride` can land exactly one past the end of the malloc'd block when `slack == 0`. That is well-defined in C, but I'd rather not rely on the reader knowing that — guard the advance on `carve_remaining > 0` and the question never arises.

**Free list:**
- `void *free_head` — head of the intrusive list threaded through dead slots. `void *` rather than a typed node, because the only thing stored in a dead slot is a `void *` and inventing a `struct rb_free_slot` would imply the slot has a layout it does not have.

**Counters:**
- `size_t slab_count`
- `size_t live`
- `size_t free_count` — free-*list* length only. `free_objs` as the spec defines it is `free_count + carve_remaining`, derived at `pool_stats` time, O(1).

---

## 2. Counter strategy

**Option A — maintained counters only.** O(1) stats. The fatal problem: `free_objs` would be derived from `free_count + carve_remaining`, `live` is a counter, `slabs` is a counter — so `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab` is checked entirely against the numbers that the same two functions just updated. It becomes close to a tautology. Concretely, a double `pool_free` increments `free_count` twice and decrements `live` twice, so the sum stays perfectly consistent *while the free list has become cyclic and one slot is now on it twice*. The spec's headline invariant would pass over exactly the bug the spec tells the reviewer to hunt for.

**Option B — on-demand free-list walk.** `free_objs` measured by walking, which is a genuinely independent observation. Costs: `pool_stats` is O(free), and the spec only requires `pool_alloc`/`pool_free` be O(1), so that is *permitted* — but asserting every op in a stress loop then becomes quadratic, and the spec wants the assertion run repeatedly under stress, not once at the end. Worse, a naive walk on a cyclic list does not report a bug; it hangs.

**Option C — maintained counters plus a debug-only bounded cross-check walk. ← recommend.** Production path is O(1). Under the debug build, `pool_stats` (or a dedicated `pool_check` helper) additionally walks the free list with a hard bound of `slab_count * objs_per_slab + 1` steps and asserts the walked length equals `free_count`. Exceeding the bound *is* the cycle report — the double-free becomes a loud, immediate failure instead of a hang or a silent pass.

How this preserves `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`:

Every slot that exists is in exactly one of three buckets — live, free-listed, uncarved — and there are exactly four state transitions in the whole file, each moving one slot between two buckets, each written as a single paired update:

| transition | updates |
|---|---|
| pop from free list | `free_count--`, `live++` |
| carve a fresh slot | `carve_remaining--`, `live++` |
| grow by one slab | `slab_count++`, `carve_remaining += objs_per_slab` |
| `pool_free` | `live--`, `free_count++` |

The first, second and fourth move a slot between buckets, so the left side is unchanged and the right side is untouched. The third adds `objs_per_slab` to both sides simultaneously — and critically, is executed **only after** `rb_malloc` has returned non-NULL, which is the "slab counted before its allocation succeeded" bug NOTES.md already names. So the invariant holds by construction; the debug walk is what keeps "by construction" from being a claim I can't check.

---

## 3. Eager vs lazy first slab — the tradeoff

**Eager (`pool_create` buys slab #1):**

- *`pool_create` failure behavior:* two fallible allocations (pool struct, then slab) ⇒ a real unwind, i.e. the goto-cleanup pattern: slab alloc fails ⇒ `rb_free` the pool struct ⇒ return NULL. One more failure path to write and to test.
- *Fault-injection surface:* `pool_create` becomes a 2-allocation scenario, so the fault sweep gets a second rung there, and the slab-alloc-fails-with-a-live-pool-struct unwind gets exercised. That is genuinely more surface, and more surface exercised is a point *for* eager.
- *Empty-pool stats:* `slabs == 1`, `live == 0`, `free_objs == objs_per_slab`. The invariant holds (`0 + 85 == 1 * 85`) and is non-trivial on a pool nobody has touched — a mildly nicer first assertion. The oddity is a pool reporting 85 free objects before anyone ever asked for one.
- *Implementation complexity:* this is where eager's apparent advantage evaporates. It does **not** remove the "no capacity, must grow" branch from `pool_alloc` — slab #2 still needs it. It only guarantees that branch isn't taken on the *first* call. So eager buys one fewer execution of an existing branch, at the price of a new failure path in `pool_create`.

**Lazy (first slab bought by the first `pool_alloc`):**

- *`pool_create` failure behavior:* exactly one allocation. `rb_malloc` returns NULL ⇒ return NULL. No unwind, no cleanup label, nothing to leak.
- *Fault-injection surface:* the first-slab failure moves from `pool_create` to the first `pool_alloc` — arguably the more interesting place to test it, because the assertion is stronger: the call must return NULL *and* leave every counter and the free list byte-identical to before, *and* a later disarmed `pool_alloc` must still succeed. An eager pool can't express that test at all, since its first slab can only fail at birth.
- *Empty-pool stats:* `slabs == 0`, `live == 0`, `free_objs == 0`; invariant is `0 + 0 == 0 * 85`, true but vacuous. Reads honestly ("nothing exists yet") at the cost of a trivially-satisfied first assertion. Also means create-then-destroy touches zero slab code — which is why slice A's destroy walk only gets real coverage in slice B.
- *Implementation complexity:* the grow condition is "free list empty **and** `carve_remaining == 0`", which is identically true for slab #1 and slab #7. Lazy's supposed extra case is the same code path, not an extra one.

The honest summary: eager trades one new failure path in `pool_create` for a slightly richer empty-pool assertion and one fewer first-call branch execution; lazy trades a vacuous empty-pool assertion for a single-allocation `pool_create` and a stronger place to test slab-allocation failure. Your call; my recommendation is in §9.

---

## 4. `pool_alloc` priority: free list → uncarved → grow

**Free list first.** Not just because popping is O(1) (carving is too), but because the alternative is wrong under the workload that matters. A steady insert/delete mix — exactly what `tests/fuzz.c` does — returns slots constantly. If carving came first, freed slots would sit unreachable until the head slab's uncarved capacity was exhausted, so the pool would keep buying slabs while holding a growing pile of reusable ones. Memory use would track total operations instead of peak live set. Free-list-first makes `slabs * objs_per_slab` track the high-water mark of `live`, which is the whole point of a slab allocator.

Secondary benefit worth stating because it shapes a test: free-list-first means a just-freed, 0xDD-poisoned slot is the *very next* slot handed out. That makes recycling — and therefore the use-after-free aliasing hazard in §6 — immediately observable in a test rather than something you hope the fuzzer stumbles into.

**Uncarved second.** Never buy memory you already own. And per §1, carving before growing is not a preference but a requirement: growing while `carve_remaining > 0` orphans the old head's uncarved slots permanently, breaking the invariant.

**Grow last.** This ordering also concentrates the only fallible step in `pool_alloc` at the bottom of the function: `pool_alloc` can return NULL on the grow path and nowhere else, and on that path no counter has been touched yet, so "leaves the pool exactly as it was" is true by position rather than by careful undo. That is the cheapest possible way to satisfy the hard constraint in CLAUDE.md.

---

## 5. `pool_free` — exactly which bytes hold the `next` pointer

The **first `sizeof(void *)` bytes of the slot**, at the slot's base address — the same address `pool_alloc` returned, byte range `[p, p + 8)`. Not at the end, not at a stored offset; the front, because that's the only location that's correct for every `stride` without extra arithmetic.

Three things make that legal, and all three are already guaranteed by the geometry slice:

1. **The slot is dead.** No live object's bytes are being aliased. This is the entire justification; it is why the trick is legitimate rather than a layout hack.
2. **It fits.** `stride >= sizeof(void *)` unconditionally — `rb_pool_geometry` applies a pointer floor even for `obj_size == 1`. So the link never spills into the neighbouring slot. (The geometry table's `obj_size 1 -> pointer floor` rows pin this.)
3. **It's aligned.** Every slot base is `alignof(max_align_t)`-aligned, hence aligned for `void *`. So this is a properly aligned store, not the kind of thing `-fsanitize=undefined` catches — and `make asan` is a gate, so had it been misaligned we'd have found out as a build-time failure rather than a mystery.

One implementation preference: do the read and the write with `memcpy` of `sizeof(void *)` bytes rather than casting to `void **` and dereferencing. The cast is alignment-legal, but the slot's bytes were last written as a `struct rb_node` and are now being read as a `void *` — a type-punned access through a different lvalue type, i.e. a strict-aliasing question I'd rather not have in the file at all. `memcpy` is exactly free at `-O1` (it compiles to one `mov`) and the question disappears. Cheap insurance, and it's one line of comment to justify.

---

## 6. Poisoning: the required order, and why ASan can't substitute

**The order in `pool_free`:**

1. `memset(slot, 0xDD, stride)` — the **whole stride**, not just `obj_size`. The intra-slot padding bytes are part of the dead slot and a stale read can land in them just as easily; and poisoning the stride keeps the rule stateless (no "poison this much, which depends on the object").
2. **Then** write the free-list `next` over `[slot, slot + 8)`.

Reversed, the `memset` lands on top of the link and destroys the free list — producing a `next` of `0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD`, which the next `pool_alloc` happily returns as a slot address. That bug is not subtle in its symptoms but it is very easy to write, because "poison it, link it" and "link it, poison it" read identically at a glance. Final resting layout of a dead slot: 8 bytes of `next`, then `stride - 8` bytes of `0xDD`.

Corollary for `pool_alloc`: read `next` out of the slot (via `memcpy`) **before** doing anything else with those bytes, and do not re-poison or zero the slot on the way out — initialization is the caller's job, and leaving the tail at `0xDD` means a caller that forgets to initialize a field sees obvious garbage rather than plausible leftovers.

**Why ASan alone cannot detect stale accesses inside a still-live slab.**

ASan's detection model is shadow memory keyed to *allocator* events: it poisons redzones around each `malloc` block and poisons the whole block on `free`. A slab is **one** `malloc` of 4096 bytes, and it stays allocated for the pool's entire lifetime. Every byte of every slot in it is therefore addressable, in-bounds, live memory from ASan's point of view, for the whole time. A read through a stale pointer to a slot that `pool_free` returned is a perfectly ordinary read of memory inside a live allocation: no shadow-byte violation, no report. Valgrind says the same thing for the same reason — the memory is addressable, and because we `memset` it, it is also *defined*, so not even a "use of uninitialised value" fires.

And there's a sharper version of the problem. Once the slot is recycled — which, per §4, is likely to be on the very next `pool_alloc` — the stale pointer now aliases a **different, live object of the same type**. There is no memory error left to detect at all; it's a legal access to live memory that happens to be the wrong object. No memory tool can see that, because nothing memory-unsafe is happening.

This is the real cost of pooling, and it's worth stating plainly in the file and in REFLECTION.md: the pool buys back per-allocation overhead by *giving up the allocator's own use-after-free detection*. `0xDD` is the compensation, and it is a weaker instrument: it doesn't report anything, it just makes a stale read return a value (`0xDDDD...`) that is an obviously invalid pointer and an obviously absurd integer, so the failure happens loudly and near the bug instead of silently and far from it.

(There *is* a way to get real detection back — ASan's manual `__asan_poison_memory_region` on each dead slot, which is precisely the hook for this case. I'd note it and decline it tonight: it's a sanitizer-specific extension, it needs `#ifdef __SANITIZE_ADDRESS__` plumbing, and it would make the poisoned-bytes test in §8 impossible to write because reading the slot would then be a reportable error. Worth one sentence in NOTES.md as a considered-and-deferred option; a candidate for a later slice if you want it.)

---

## 7. `pool_destroy`

It frees **slabs, never objects** — and that is why live objects are not a problem. The pool owns slabs; each slab is exactly one `rb_malloc` block; one `rb_free` of that block releases all of its slots at once, regardless of whether each was live, free-listed, or never carved. There is no per-object bookkeeping to unwind, no free list to unlink, no need to know how many objects were live. That's the same property that makes the invariant three-state rather than per-slot.

**The exact pointer that must be saved before `rb_free`: `slab->next`.** The chain header is in-band at the front of the very block being released, so the loop must read `next` out of the slab, *then* free the slab, *then* advance. Reading `slab->next` after `rb_free(slab)` is a genuine use-after-free of a real `malloc` block — which is the one place in this whole design where ASan and valgrind *will* catch the mistake, precisely because the slab itself is an allocator object. Same shape as the HW1 right-spine teardown rule ("save the pointer before you free the thing that contains it"), one level down, as NOTES.md already anticipated.

Three more points:

- `free_head` and `carve_next` point *into* slabs. They are dangling the moment the first slab is freed, so they must not be read after the loop starts. Don't walk the free list in `pool_destroy` — there is nothing to do with it, and walking it is a use-after-free waiting to be added by a well-meaning cleanup.
- The pool struct is its own allocation; `rb_free` it after the chain walk, not before (it holds the chain head).
- Make `pool_destroy(NULL)` a no-op, mirroring `rb_destroy`'s documented NULL-safety. This is not cosmetic: it makes `rb_create_pooled`'s own failure unwind on Evening 6 a single unconditional call.

**Scope flag for Evening 6, not tonight:** `pool_destroy` knows nothing about keys, values, or `value_free`. When a pooled tree is torn down, `rb_destroy` must still walk the tree and release every key copy and owned value *before* the pool is destroyed — the pool reclaims node *storage*, not the heap the nodes point at. Keys will still come from `rb_malloc` directly. Mentioning it now so it doesn't look like an oversight tonight.

**One contract to document now:** `pool_free` cannot validate its argument. Checking "does this pointer belong to this pool and is it not already free" requires a slab scan or a free-list scan, and either destroys the O(1) requirement. So the contract is explicitly: *a pointer previously returned by `pool_alloc` on this pool, not already freed.* A violation is undefined behavior the pool does not detect at the point of the call — the debug cross-check walk from §2 catches the double-free case shortly *after* the fact, which is the best O(1) allows. Write that in the file; a reviewer will ask.

---

## 8. Tests

**Getting at `objs_per_slab` without circularity.** The test calls `rb_pool_geometry` — and that is *not* circular, because the geometry formula is already independently pinned by 20 rows of hand-worked literals in `geom_cases[]`. Belt-and-braces: the pool tests use one fixed `obj_size` (48, the current node size) and assert `objs_per_slab == 85` against a literal once, up front. If geometry ever changes, that single assertion fails loudly instead of the pool tests silently re-deriving a wrong capacity and agreeing with themselves.

**Shared helper.** `check_pool_invariant(p, label)`: asserts `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`, and under test hooks also runs the bounded free-list walk cross-check from §2. Called after **every** scenario below and after every op in the stress loop — per the spec's "the earliest assertion failure is usually much more informative than the corpse."

## 9. Recommended decisions

1. **Fields** as in §1: cached geometry (`obj_size`, `stride`, `slot0_offset`, `objs_per_slab`; no `slack`), `slabs` head, `carve_next`/`carve_remaining`, `free_head`, and three counters `slab_count`/`live`/`free_count`.
2. **Counters: option C** — maintained counters for O(1) stats, plus a debug-only free-list walk bounded by `slab_count * objs_per_slab + 1` that cross-checks `free_count` and reports a cycle on overrun. Option A alone makes the spec's headline invariant nearly vacuous against a double free.
3. **First slab: lazy** — recommended, your call. Deciding factors: `pool_create` stays a single allocation with no unwind, and the slab-allocation-failure test gets strictly stronger (pool survives the failure and still works afterward, which eager cannot express). The cost is a vacuous empty-pool assertion, which the other scenarios more than make up for.
4. **`pool_alloc` order:** free list → uncarved → grow, with growth the only fallible step and the last thing in the function.
5. **Link location:** first `sizeof(void *)` bytes of the slot, read and written with `memcpy`.
6. **Poison the full `stride` with `0xDD`, then write the link.** Unconditional in all builds, behind one compile-time escape hatch — so there is exactly one code path that is actually tested, rather than a debug build the tests exercise and a production build nobody does. Decline ASan manual poisoning tonight; record it in NOTES.md as considered and deferred.
7. **`pool_destroy`:** save `slab->next` before each `rb_free`; never touch `free_head`/`carve_next` during teardown; free the pool struct last; NULL-safe.
8. **`pool_stats`:** tolerate NULL out-parameters (write only what's asked for — three `if`s, and tests usually want one number); require a non-NULL pool.
9. **`pool_create` with an `obj_size` geometry rejects** returns NULL. This is the open question NOTES.md deferred; resolving it here means `rb_pool_geometry`'s boolean is checked at exactly one site in the program.

STATE: HW2 M1 is green and committed (`a250531`, `a8f4439`): the allocation seam is wired and the fault sweep runs. `src/pool.c` is still empty; `rb_create_pooled` and `rb_snapshot` are declared in the frozen header and unimplemented. This session was explicitly exploration-only — no source, tests, or Makefile touched.
DID: re-read the Mutation 2 material end to end rather than working from the summary — §8's preamble on the three accumulating contracts, the companion discussion of per-allocation overhead and slabs (pp. 10–11, incl. the `kmem_cache`/Solaris lineage), §8.2's API and constraints, Figure 4 and its caption, the "what still comes from `rb_malloc`" paragraph, the ASan/poisoning discussion, the M2 rubric row, and the spec's own adversarial-review prompt for M2. Worked through what an `rb_pool_t` owns (slabs, a carve cursor, a free-list head), the three states a slot can be in (live / free-listed / uncarved), why the intrusive `next` may legally live in a dead object's own bytes (the slot is dead, big enough, and — given the stride — aligned enough), why `pool_alloc`/`pool_free` are O(1) (all deciding happened at `pool_create`; no size search, no coalescing, and no object->slab lookup on the hot path), and why `pool_destroy` can release whole slabs with live objects in them (the pool owns slabs, not objects). Then laid out the three decisions the spec leaves open, with tradeoffs and failure paths for each, and did not choose.
DECIDED: (1) slots are aligned to `_Alignof(max_align_t)`, with the stride `obj_size` rounded up to that alignment and never below `sizeof(void *)`, so every slot address is aligned rather than only slot 0 — the pool cannot be told its caller's alignment (`pool_create` takes only `obj_size`), so it promises one conservatively; noted explicitly that this is fundamental alignment and NOT support for over-aligned (`_Alignas`-beyond-`max_align_t`) types. (2) slab metadata lives in-band at the front of each slab, accepting the payload cost and the "header eats bytes the naive division forgets" off-by-one in exchange for one `rb_malloc` per slab and therefore one failure point when the pool grows, instead of out-of-band's second allocation with its own unwind path. (3) `free_objs` follows the spec's operational definition — free-list slots plus uncarved capacity in existing slabs — giving `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. Full reasoning, costs accepted, and consequences recorded in NOTES.md under HW2 "Choices left up to me".
LEARNED: the two layers of Figure 4 are the useful separation — slab layout answers "where is the storage?" and is fixed arithmetic, while free-list policy answers "which slot next?" and ignores physical layout entirely; keeping them apart means geometry and history can be tested independently. Also that "pooled tree" does not mean "no ordinary allocation": nodes come from the pool, but key copies stay variable-length and keep coming from `rb_malloc`, which is why pooled teardown can return node storage wholesale yet still has to visit every node. And that the spec's in-band selling point of answering "which slab is this?" by masking does not actually hold here, because `rb_malloc` forwards to `malloc` and guarantees `max_align_t` alignment, not page alignment — so that benefit was excluded from the justification rather than claimed.

STATE: the geometry slice is green and committed (`febfdc2`); `src/pool.c` held `rb_pool_geometry` and the in-band `struct rb_slab` and nothing else. The four questions the previous evening left open (counter strategy, eager vs. lazy first slab, NULL tolerance in `pool_stats`, what `pool_create` does with a rejected `obj_size`) were all answered before any code was written, because every one of them shapes the struct.
IMPLEMENTED NOW (slice A): `struct rb_pool` with its full field set, `pool_create`, `pool_stats`, `pool_destroy`. `pool_create` computes the geometry *before* allocating and caches all four numbers, so it has exactly one fallible step and no unwind path; a rejected `obj_size` returns NULL having spent no `rb_malloc` call at all. `pool_stats` is three maintained counters (one of them the sum `free_count + carve_remaining`) and is O(1). `pool_destroy` walks the slab chain saving `slab->next` before each `rb_free`, then releases the pool struct. A pool built by this slice owns no slabs and can hand nothing out: `live` is always 0 and the invariant always reads `0 + 0 == 0 * objs_per_slab`.
PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED (and deliberately absent from this commit): `pool_alloc`, `pool_free`, slab growth, slot carving, the intrusive free list, 0xDD debug poisoning, the bounded debug cross-check walk that will keep `free_count` honest, and `rb_create_pooled`. Three fields (`carve_next`, `free_head`, and `free_count` beyond its appearance in the `pool_stats` sum) are written by `pool_create` and read by nothing yet — the whole struct went in at once so later slices add behavior without churning the layout, and the comments name which slice claims each field. `pool_destroy`'s chain walk — the save-`next`-before-`rb_free` rule that is the entire point of the function — is therefore written but unexercised until slabs exist in slice B.
DID: implemented the three functions in `src/pool.c`; added five scenarios plus `check_pool_invariant()` and `pool_capacity()` to `tests/test_rbtree.c` (31 pool assertions, 805 total in the unit binary). Mutation-tested the new assertions the same way the geometry slice was, compiling broken scratch copies of `pool.c` against the unmodified test: moving the geometry check after the allocation (allocate-then-discard) failed 4 assertions, making `pool_stats` report a slab-less pool's capacity as if eager failed 9, and dropping `rb_free(p)` from `pool_destroy` failed **zero** assertions and was caught only by valgrind (440 bytes definitely lost in 5 blocks). Full battery green from a clean rebuild each time: `make test` 805 assertions + 100,000 fuzz ops, `make asan` (address+undefined) clean, `make memcheck` 0 errors with 610/610 allocs/frees on the unit binary and 20,010/20,010 on the fuzzer.
DECIDED: (1) **lazy first slab.** `pool_create` buys no slab. The decisive argument was not the saved allocation but that eager buys nothing: the "no capacity, grow" branch `pool_alloc` needs for slab 2 is the same branch it needs for slab 1, so eager would have added a second failure path and a real unwind to `pool_create` in exchange for one fewer execution of a branch that has to exist anyway. It also moves first-slab-allocation-failure to a strictly stronger test site — a `pool_alloc` that must return NULL, leave every counter untouched, and still work once the injector is disarmed, which an eager pool cannot express because its first slab can only fail at birth. Cost accepted: the empty-pool invariant assertion is vacuous (`0 + 0 == 0 * 85`) rather than merely trivial. (2) **maintained counters plus a bounded debug cross-check** (the walk lands with the free list in slice C). Option A alone was rejected on a specific ground, not a general one: with `free_objs` derived as `free_count + carve_remaining`, the headline invariant would be checked entirely against the numbers the mutators just updated, and a double `pool_free` increments `free_count` twice while decrementing `live` twice — so the sum stays consistent while the free list goes cyclic, i.e. the invariant would pass over exactly the bug the spec's M2 review prompt tells the reviewer to hunt. An on-demand walk was rejected because it makes per-op assertion quadratic under stress and, on a cyclic list, hangs instead of reporting. (4) **`pool_create` returns NULL for an `obj_size` geometry rejects**, which resolves the internal-only contract the geometry slice deliberately left open; checking the helper's boolean here means it is checked at exactly one site in the whole program. (5) `rb_pool_t` is declared **incomplete** in the test (`typedef struct rb_pool rb_pool_t;` plus three prototypes) — unlike the geometry helper's out-parameters, there is no layout to duplicate across the file boundary at all, so there is nothing that can drift.

Writing the check now anyway is still right (no scenario gets added without it), but "the invariant passes" is worth nothing until slice B gives it non-zero terms, and saying so in the log is more useful than letting a green line imply coverage it does not have. The mutation run made the same point from the other side: the one mutant the test file could not catch was the leaked pool struct, which only valgrind sees — so `make memcheck` is not a formality on this file, it is the only detector for a whole class of `pool_destroy` bug. Also a design observation worth keeping: deciding the counter strategy *before* the struct was not bureaucratic sequencing, since option B (on-demand walk) would have needed no `free_count` field at all and option C needs it plus a walk helper — the struct is downstream of that choice, and writing it first would have meant rewriting it.
NEXT FIRST STEP: slice B — slab growth and carving behind `pool_alloc`, in the approved order (free list → uncarved → grow) with growth as the only fallible step and the last statement in the function, so "leaves the pool exactly as it was" holds by position rather than by undo. First assertions to write: fill exactly one slab and confirm the 86th allocation buys a second slab rather than handing out the tail slack.
OPEN: `pool_alloc`, `pool_free`, the intrusive free list, 0xDD debug poisoning (debug-gated, not unconditional — the rubric asks for debug poisoning and the spec does not support making it unconditional), the bounded cross-check walk, `rb_create_pooled`, and re-running the whole HW1 + M1 battery on the pooled build. Unresolved and worth a decision in slice B: whether `memcheck` should depend on `clean` in the Makefile, since the ASan-binary staleness trap recorded in the 2026-10-07 entry bit again tonight and a false green from it is a real risk. Also still owed: the `kmem_cache` comparison paragraph in REFLECTION.md.
EOF

content.text:
CLAUDE.md requires a plan and approval before editing for anything algorithmic or multi-file, so here is slice B tightly — you approved the shape already, this is just the specifics.

## Slice B: growth + carving behind `pool_alloc`

**`static bool pool_grow(rb_pool_t *p)`** — one `rb_malloc(RB_SLAB_BYTES)`. On NULL: return false having mutated **nothing**. On success: push LIFO onto the chain, `slab_count++`, `carve_next = (unsigned char *)slab + slot0_offset`, `carve_remaining = objs_per_slab`. Asserts `carve_remaining == 0` on entry, since growing earlier strands the old head's uncarved slots.

**`void *pool_alloc(rb_pool_t *p)`** — in slice B: if `carve_remaining == 0`, grow (bail to NULL on failure); then carve. The free-list pop goes in *front* of this in slice C; I'm not adding it now as a dead branch, because `free_head` is permanently NULL tonight and it would be untestable. The grow attempt sits before any counter mutation, so "a failed `pool_alloc` leaves the pool exactly as it was" holds by position, with nothing to undo.

Carve step: take `carve_next`, `carve_remaining--`, advance `carve_next += stride` unconditionally, `live++`. The unconditional advance can leave `carve_next` at most one byte past the slab's end when `slack == 0` — a legal pointer value that is never dereferenced, because `carve_remaining == 0` gates every read of it and growth resets it. The alternative (skip the final advance) leaves the cursor pointing *at* the last handed-out slot, which I like less: monotone is easier to reason about than "sometimes stale." Say if you'd rather have the guard.

**Not in this slice:** `pool_free`, the free list, 0xDD poisoning, the cross-check walk. A carved slot therefore contains raw `malloc` garbage and is the caller's to initialize — poisoning arrives in C.

**Tests** (`tests/test_rbtree.c`, same hooks block):

| | asserts |
|---|---|
| first alloc | non-NULL, `max_align_t`-aligned, `1/1/84`, invariant |
| fill one slab | 85 allocs, all distinct, all aligned, **consecutive addresses exactly `stride` apart and ascending** (this is what pins the carve arithmetic), then `1/85/0` |
| the 86th alloc | `2/86/84` — a slab bought rather than the tail slack handed out |
| no per-object allocation | filling one slab costs exactly **1** `rb_malloc` beyond create, via `fault_alloc_total()` |
| write-through | write a distinct byte pattern into all `obj_size` bytes of every slot across two slabs, read every one back — the real detector for overlapping slots, which pointer-distinctness alone would miss if `stride` were too small |
| `objs_per_slab == 1` (obj_size 4080) | every alloc buys a slab; `free_objs` is 0 throughout |
| grow failure ×2 | injected on the *first* slab (`0/0/0` before and after) and on a *later* slab (carve exhausted, `1/85/0` before and after); both return NULL, both keep the invariant, and both still work once disarmed |
| destroy with live objects | 170 live across two slabs, then `pool_destroy` — leaks adjudicated by asan/memcheck |

That last row finally exercises `pool_destroy`'s chain walk, so I'll also mutation-test the save-`next`-before-`rb_free` rule (reading `slab->next` after the free should now be a reportable ASan use-after-free) alongside the usual mutants for the slack off-by-one and the grow-ordering.

Files: `src/pool.c`, `tests/test_rbtree.c`. Nothing else — no Makefile, no NOTES.md, header untouched. Commit on your go after I show the diff and the three gates: `M2: slab growth and carving behind pool_alloc`.

Approve and I'll build it.

 * caller's to initialize; and because nothing can be returned yet, live only

/* Buys one slab and makes it the carve head. Returns false having mutated
 * NOTHING if the allocation fails -- which is what lets pool_alloc's failure
 * path be a bare `return NULL` with no unwinding to do.
 *
 * Only ever called with the head slab fully carved: growing while the old
 * head still had uncarved slots would strand them, since one cursor pair can
 * only track one slab. That is the "slot lost on the floor" the invariant
 * live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab exists to catch, so it is
 * asserted here rather than left as a comment. */
static bool pool_grow(rb_pool_t *p)
{
    assert(p->carve_remaining == 0);

    struct rb_slab *slab = rb_malloc(RB_SLAB_BYTES);
    if (slab == NULL) return false;

    slab->next         = p->slabs;   /* LIFO: the newest slab is the carve head */
    p->slabs           = slab;
    p->slab_count++;
    p->carve_next      = (unsigned char *)slab + p->slot0_offset;
    p->carve_remaining = p->objs_per_slab;
    return true;
}

/* Returns one slot, or NULL if the pool must grow and cannot. O(1): no size
 * search, no coalescing, and no object->slab lookup -- every decision was
 * made once, in pool_create.
 *
 * The slot's bytes are uninitialized. p must be non-NULL.
 *
 * Order: uncarved capacity, then grow. SLICE C inserts the free-list pop
 * ahead of both, which is where reuse-before-carving starts to matter; today
 * free_head is permanently NULL, so that branch would be dead code and is
 * not written yet.
 *
 * The one fallible step is the grow, and it happens before any counter is
 * touched, so "a failed pool_alloc leaves the pool exactly as it was" holds
 * by position rather than by undoing anything. */
void *pool_alloc(rb_pool_t *p)
{
    assert(p != NULL);

    if (p->carve_remaining == 0 && !pool_grow(p))
        return NULL;

    /* Invariant: carve_next addresses an uncarved slot whenever
     * carve_remaining > 0, which the branch above has just guaranteed. The
     * advance is unconditional, so the cursor stays monotone; after the last
     * slot of a slab it holds the slab's one-past-the-end address when
     * slack == 0, which is a legal pointer value that is never dereferenced
     * because carve_remaining == 0 gates every read of it, and the next grow
     * resets it into a fresh slab. */
    void *slot = p->carve_next;
    p->carve_remaining--;
    p->carve_next += p->stride;
    p->live++;

    return slot;
}

+    check(live == cap, "[pool: fill] every slot in the slab is live");
+    check(free_objs == 0, "[pool: fill] a full slab reports no reusable slots");
+    /* The 86th: must buy a slab, NOT hand out the tail slack. */
+    check(slots[cap] != NULL, "[pool: cross] the allocation past a full slab succeeds");
+    check(slabs == 2, "[pool: cross] crossing a full slab buys a second slab");
+    check(live == cap + 1, "[pool: cross] the new slot is live");
+    check(free_objs == cap - 1, "[pool: cross] the new slab's remaining slots are free");
+    /* Fill the second slab too: it must yield exactly cap slots as well. */
+    for (size_t i = cap + 1; i < POOL_TWO_SLABS; i++) {
+    check(nulls == 0, "[pool: two slabs] the second slab fills without failure");
+    check(slabs == 2, "[pool: two slabs] two full slabs, no third bought");
+    check(live == POOL_TWO_SLABS, "[pool: two slabs] every slot in both slabs is live");
+    check(free_objs == 0, "[pool: two slabs] two full slabs report no reusable slots");
+/* The point of a slab allocator: object count does not drive allocation
+ * count. Measured as a delta across the run rather than against an absolute
+ * total, so the claim does not depend on what any earlier test allocated. */
+    fault_alloc_arm(100000); /* resets the counter; nothing here comes near 100000 */
+    check(p != NULL, "[pool: malloc count] pool_create succeeds with the injector idle");
+    check(nulls == 0, "[pool: malloc count] filling the first slab succeeds");
+          "[pool: malloc count] filling a whole slab costs exactly one rb_malloc");
+    check(pool_alloc(p) != NULL, "[pool: malloc count] the allocation past the slab succeeds");
+          "[pool: malloc count] crossing into a second slab costs exactly one more rb_malloc");
+/* Distinct pointers are not enough: if the stride were smaller than the
+ * object, adjacent slots would overlap while still having distinct
+ * addresses. Writing a per-slot pattern across every byte of every slot and
+ * reading them all back afterwards is what actually detects that. */
+    check(nulls == 0, "[pool: overlap] two slabs' worth of allocations succeed");
+          "[pool: overlap] every slot's full object_size bytes survive writes to every other slot");
+/* The degenerate geometry: one slot per slab, so every single allocation
+ * must buy a slab and free_objs is never anything but zero. */
+    check(objs == 1, "[pool: one-per-slab] a 4080-byte object leaves exactly one slot per slab");
+                 "[pool: one-per-slab] allocation %zu leaves %zu slabs / %zu live / 0 free",
+        check(slabs == i && live == i && free_objs == 0, msg);
+/* Growth is the only fallible step in pool_alloc, and this is the stronger
+ * test site that choosing a lazy first slab bought: the FIRST slab's
+ * allocation can be injected to fail on a pool that already exists, so the
+ * assertion is not just "NULL" but "unchanged, and still usable afterwards".
+ * An eager pool could only have failed this at birth. */
+    check(p != NULL, "[pool: grow-fail first] pool_create succeeds before arming");
+    check(slot == NULL, "[pool: grow-fail first] pool_alloc returns NULL when the slab fails");
+          "[pool: grow-fail first] exactly one allocation was attempted");
+          "[pool: grow-fail first] the pool is untouched by the failed allocation");
+    check(slot != NULL, "[pool: grow-fail first] the pool still works once disarmed");
+          "[pool: grow-fail first] the retry produces normal stats");
+/* The same failure one slab in, where there is real state to preserve: a
+ * full slab, a live count of cap, and an exhausted carve cursor. */
+    check(p != NULL, "[pool: grow-fail later] pool_create succeeds");
+    check(nulls == 0, "[pool: grow-fail later] the first slab fills before arming");
+    check(slot == NULL, "[pool: grow-fail later] pool_alloc returns NULL when the slab fails");
+          "[pool: grow-fail later] the full slab and its counters are untouched");
+    check(slot != NULL, "[pool: grow-fail later] the pool still grows once disarmed");
+          "[pool: grow-fail later] the retry buys the second slab");
+/* pool_destroy with every slot still live, which is the case the design is
+ * built for: the pool owns slabs, not objects, so live slots are released
+ * wholesale with the slab that contains them. This is also the first
+ * scenario in which pool_destroy's chain walk actually runs -- the
+ * save-next-before-rb_free rule is unexercised until a pool owns slabs.
+ * The leak claim itself is adjudicated by make asan / make memcheck. */

+    check(1, "[pool: destroy-live] pool_destroy over two full slabs did not crash");

+    check(nulls == 0, "[pool: destroy-partial] one full slab plus one slot of the next");
+    check(1, "[pool: destroy-partial] pool_destroy over a partly carved slab did not crash");

## `src/pool.c` (+82, shown in full above)

`pool_grow` — one `rb_malloc`, returns false having mutated nothing on failure, asserts the head slab is fully carved on entry. `pool_alloc` — carve-then-grow, grow attempted before any counter is touched, unconditional monotonic cursor advance. Both adjustments applied: the comment says the cursor "holds the slab's **one-past-the-end address** when `slack == 0`, which is a legal pointer value that is never dereferenced," and the allocation-count test uses before/after deltas.

## Mutation checks — and one found a real gap

| mutant | failures |
|---|---|
| b1 tail slack handed out (`objs_per_slab + 1`) | 67 |
| b2 grow on every allocation | 111 |
| b3 slab counted before `rb_malloc` succeeds | 118 |
| b4 cursor advanced by `obj_size` instead of `stride` | **0 → 4 after a fix** |
| b5 `pool_destroy` reads `slab->next` after `rb_free` | 0 assertions; **ASan heap-use-after-free**, READ of size 8 |

**b4 initially passed the entire suite.** Every `obj_size` the approved tests used — 48 and 4080 — happens to have `stride == obj_size`, so advancing by the wrong quantity was invisible, and no carving test exercised nonzero `slack` either, which is precisely what the cursor comment reasons about. I added one scenario beyond the approved plan to close both: `test_pool_alloc_stride_is_not_obj_size`, over `obj_size` 40 (stride 48, no slack) and 17 (stride 32, slack 16), asserting consecutive slots step by `stride` and that the slack never becomes an 86th/128th slot. It asserts `stride != obj_size` up front, so the test can't silently become vacuous the way the others had. That's the one addition you haven't signed off on — say if you'd rather it went in slice C instead.

b5 is the one worth noting for the log: the save-`next`-before-`rb_free` rule was unexercised until tonight, and it is detectable *only* by ASan — no assertion in the test file catches it.

## Battery, clean rebuild before each

- `make test`: 1004 assertions pass (805 → 1004), 100,000 fuzz ops OK
- `make asan` (address+undefined): clean
- `make memcheck`: 0 errors, **642/642** allocs/frees unit, 20,172/20,172 fuzzer

Committed as `0ebee46`, working tree clean.

Contents: `src/pool.c` and `tests/test_rbtree.c` only — **no DEVLOG entry**, since you asked for that explicitly last round and didn't this time. The slice B record (the lazy-pool payoff at the grow-failure test site, the b4 gap and why the suite was blind to it, b5 being ASan-only) isn't written down anywhere but this conversation yet. Say the word and I'll add it as its own commit.

Milestone commit count is now 8 since HW2 started, well clear of the spec's ≥ 8 floor for the whole assignment.

Slice C next when you want it: the intrusive free list, `pool_free`, debug-gated 0xDD poisoning, and the bounded cross-check walk — the slice where the invariant finally stops being satisfiable by zeroes, and where `free_list → uncarved → grow` ordering starts to matter.

Slice C plan — the one decision that needs your call is the poison gate, since you corrected me on it earlier.

## Slice C: free list, `pool_free`, debug poisoning, cross-check walk

**The debug gate: `#ifndef NDEBUG`** (recommended). It's the notion of "debug build" this file already uses for `assert`, needs no new macro and no Makefile change, and leaves poisoning plus the cross-check walk active in all four current build modes — `test`, `asan`, `memcheck`, and the fuzzer's production build, which is where reuse actually churns. Anyone wanting a measurement-only build gets `-DNDEBUG` and both compile out. The alternatives are worse: `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` is unit-binary-only, so the fuzzer would never poison; a fresh `RB_POOL_DEBUG` macro that nothing defines is just "always off" with extra steps, and defining it would need the Makefile edit you ruled out.

**`pool_free(rb_pool_t *p, void *obj)`** — in order: `memset(obj, 0xDD, stride)` over the **full stride** (debug only), then `memcpy` the old `free_head` into the first `sizeof(void *)` bytes, then `free_head = obj`, `free_count++`, `live--`. Asserts `p->live > 0`, which catches a free against an empty pool for free. The reverse order destroys the link with 0xDD, which is the bug the ordering exists to avoid.

**`pool_alloc`** gains the pop in front of the carve: `memcpy` the link out, `free_head = next`, `free_count--`, `live++`. The popped slot keeps its stale link bytes and its 0xDD tail — initialization stays the caller's job, as with a carved slot.

**`pool_free_list_agrees(p)`** (`#ifndef NDEBUG`) — walks the list bounded by `slab_count * objs_per_slab + 1` and returns false on overrun or on a length that disagrees with `free_count`. Called via `assert` from `pool_stats`, so every existing `check_pool_invariant` call cross-checks it, and slice D's stress loop gets it for free. The bound is what turns a cyclic list into a report instead of a hang.

**Tests** — the invariant finally stops being satisfiable by zeroes:

| | asserts |
|---|---|
| free one slot | `live` down 1, `free_objs` up 1, invariant |
| **reuse priority** | with uncarved capacity *and* a non-empty free list, the next alloc returns the **freed** slot, not a fresh one — this is what pins the ordering |
| reuse costs nothing | free *k*, alloc *k*: zero `rb_malloc` (delta), `slabs` unchanged, every pointer from the freed set |
| LIFO | free a, b, c → alloc returns c, b, a |
| spill to carve | free 3, alloc 4: first three from the list, fourth from uncarved, no allocation either way |
| **`free_objs` has two live terms** | 1 live + 1 freed + uncarved → `free_objs == free_count + carve_remaining`; dropping either term now fails. This closes the slice-A gap I logged as unfalsifiable |
| poison bytes | after a free, bytes `[sizeof(void *), stride)` are all `0xDD`; `[0, 8)` is the link and is not asserted |
| poison covers the stride | same check at `obj_size` 40 (stride 48) out to `stride - 1`, pinning "memset the stride, not the object" |
| full cycle | fill two slabs, free all 170 → `live == 0`, `free_objs == 170`; realloc all 170 with zero new slabs |
| destroy with a populated free list | mixed live / free-listed / uncarved, leaks adjudicated by asan + memcheck |

Mutants I'll run: link-then-poison, `memset` of `obj_size` instead of `stride`, a dropped `live--`/`free_count++`, carve-before-pop, and a pop that doesn't advance `free_head`. The cross-check walk gets demonstrated against a deliberate double `pool_free` in a **scratch program**, not in the suite — a double free is undefined per `pool_free`'s contract, so the suite shouldn't perform one, and `assert` aborts rather than returning something a test could check.

Files: `src/pool.c`, `tests/test_rbtree.c`. Nothing else. Then mutants, restore, clean `test`/`asan`/`memcheck`, and stop before committing — `M2: intrusive free list, pool_free, debug poisoning`.

Approve the `#ifndef NDEBUG` gate (or name a different one) and I'll build it.

"""
new=""" * Four slices live here so far: the slot geometry (the arithmetic that
 * divides one page-sized slab into aligned, fixed-size slots), the pool
 * lifecycle (pool_create / pool_stats / pool_destroy), slab growth plus slot
 * carving behind pool_alloc, and the intrusive free list behind pool_free
 * with its 0xDD debug poisoning. The allocator is now complete; what remains
 * for later slices is rb_create_pooled and the stress/fault battery over it.
"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)

# includes
old="#include <stdbool.h>\n#include <stddef.h>\n"
new="#include <stdbool.h>\n#include <stddef.h>\n#include <string.h>\n"
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)

# pool_alloc: free-list pop ahead of the carve, and retire the stale note
old=""" * Order: uncarved capacity, then grow. SLICE C inserts the free-list pop
 * ahead of both, which is where reuse-before-carving starts to matter; today
 * free_head is permanently NULL, so that branch would be dead code and is
 * not written yet.
 *
 * The one fallible step is the grow, and it happens before any counter is
 * touched, so "a failed pool_alloc leaves the pool exactly as it was" holds
 * by position rather than by undoing anything. */
void *pool_alloc(rb_pool_t *p)
{
    assert(p != NULL);

    if (p->carve_remaining == 0 && !pool_grow(p))
        return NULL;
"""
new=""" * Order: free list, then uncarved capacity, then grow. Reuse comes first so
 * that slabs track the high-water mark of live rather than the total number
 * of operations -- carving first would leave freed slots unreachable until a
 * slab was exhausted, and an insert/delete workload would keep buying slabs
 * while holding a growing pile of reusable ones.
 *
 * The one fallible step is the grow, and it happens before any counter is
 * touched, so "a failed pool_alloc leaves the pool exactly as it was" holds
 * by position rather than by undoing anything. */
void *pool_alloc(rb_pool_t *p)
{
    assert(p != NULL);

    if (p->free_head != NULL) {
        /* The dead slot's first bytes are the link, not an object; read it
         * out before the slot is handed back to a caller who will overwrite
         * it. memcpy rather than a cast, for the reason pool_free gives. */
        void *slot = p->free_head;
        void *next;
        memcpy(&next, slot, sizeof next);

        p->free_head = next;
        p->free_count--;
        p->live++;

        /* The slot still carries its stale link and its 0xDD tail. Clearing
         * them is not this function's job: a carved slot is uninitialized
         * too, and a caller that forgets to initialize should find obvious
         * garbage rather than plausible zeroes. */
        return slot;
    }

    if (p->carve_remaining == 0 && !pool_grow(p))
        return NULL;
"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)

# slice C block, inserted before pool_stats
anchor="/* Reports the three numbers the M2 invariant is stated over."
block = r'''/* ------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * SLICE C: the intrusive free list, pool_free, and 0xDD debug poisoning.
 *
 * What remains after this slice: rb_create_pooled, and re-running the whole
 * HW1 + M1 battery over a pooled tree.
 *
 * Both the poisoning and the free-list cross-check below are gated on
 * NDEBUG -- the same notion of a "debug build" that assert already uses in
 * this file, so there is no new knob and no build machinery. With the
 * Makefile never defining NDEBUG they are active in every build the project
 * actually produces (test, asan, memcheck, and the fuzzer), which is where
 * they are wanted; -DNDEBUG compiles both out for a measurement-only build.
 */

#define RB_POOL_POISON 0xDD

#ifndef NDEBUG
/* Measures the free list independently of free_count, which is the whole
 * point: the three numbers pool_stats reports are maintained counters, so
 * live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab is otherwise checked against the
 * same values that pool_alloc and pool_free just produced. A double
 * pool_free, for instance, decrements live twice and increments free_count
 * twice -- the sum stays consistent while the same slot sits on the list
 * twice and the list has become cyclic.
 *
 * Returns false if the walk disagrees with free_count, or if it runs past
 * the number of slots that exist at all.
 *
 * O(free list), so this is debug-only and deliberately not on the alloc/free
 * path, which must stay O(1). */
static bool pool_free_list_agrees(const rb_pool_t *p)
{
    size_t bound = p->slab_count * p->objs_per_slab + 1;
    size_t n     = 0;
    void  *cur   = p->free_head;

    /* Invariant: n counts the slots already stepped over, and the step that
     * would push it past bound reports instead of taking it -- so a cyclic
     * list is a finite false, not an infinite walk. */
    while (cur != NULL) {
        if (++n > bound) return false;
        memcpy(&cur, cur, sizeof cur);
    }

    return n == p->free_count;
}
#endif

/* Returns one slot to the pool. O(1), and indifferent to which slab the slot
 * came from -- a single intrusive list is what buys that.
 *
 * CONTRACT, and it cannot be checked here: obj must be a pointer pool_alloc
 * returned from this pool and not already freed. Verifying either would need
 * a scan of the slabs or of the free list, which is exactly the O(1) the
 * allocator exists to provide. A violation is undefined behavior at the point
 * of the call; the debug cross-check above catches the double-free case
 * shortly afterwards, at the next pool_stats, which is the best O(1) allows.
 *
 * The link lives in the first sizeof(void *) bytes of the slot. That is legal
 * because the slot is dead (no live object's bytes are aliased), because the
 * geometry's pointer floor guarantees stride >= sizeof(void *) so it cannot
 * spill into the neighbour, and because every slot base is max_align_t
 * aligned and so aligned for void *. It is written with memcpy rather than
 * through a cast: these bytes were last written as some caller's object and
 * are now read as a void *, which is a type-punned access a cast would make
 * the compiler's business and memcpy does not. At -O1 it is one store. */
void pool_free(rb_pool_t *p, void *obj)
{
    assert(p != NULL && obj != NULL);
    assert(p->live > 0); /* nothing is live, so obj cannot have come from here */

#ifndef NDEBUG
    /* Poison FIRST, then write the link over the front. The reverse order
     * overwrites the link with 0xDD and corrupts the list -- the next
     * pool_alloc would return 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD as a slot address. The full
     * stride is poisoned, not obj_size: the inter-slot padding belongs to the
     * dead slot too, and a stale read can land in it just as easily. */
    memset(obj, RB_POOL_POISON, p->stride);
#endif

    memcpy(obj, &p->free_head, sizeof p->free_head);
    p->free_head = obj;
    p->free_count++;

content.text:
Slice C built and verified. **Stopped before committing.**

## `src/pool.c` (+132)

- **`pool_free`** — poison the full stride (`#ifndef NDEBUG`), *then* `memcpy` the link into the first `sizeof(void *)` bytes, then push and adjust counters. Asserts `live > 0`. The contract (a pointer from this pool, not already freed) is documented as uncheckable in O(1).
- **`pool_alloc`** — free-list pop ahead of the carve, link read out with `memcpy`; the slot keeps its stale link and `0xDD` tail, since initialization is the caller's job either way.
- **`pool_free_list_agrees`** (`#ifndef NDEBUG`) — bounded walk, asserted from `pool_stats`, so every existing `check_pool_invariant` call now cross-checks it.

Both gates verified in both states: the normal build has 1260 assertions, `-DNDEBUG` compiles clean under `-Werror` and passes with 1246 (the 14 poison assertions compile out).

## Mutants

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| c1 link-then-poison | **segfault** — the walk dereferences `0xDD…` as a link. Detected, but as a crash rather than a clean failure |
| c2 `memset` of `obj_size` instead of `stride` | **escaped → 1 failure after a test fix** (below) |
| c3 dropped `live--` | 187 failures |
| c4 dropped `free_count++` | 0 assertions — **caught only by the cross-check walk** (abort) |
| c5 priority inversion (carve before reuse) | 11 failures |
| c7 pop without advancing `free_head` | 0 assertions — **caught only by the cross-check walk** (abort) |

=== REFLECTION.md in full ===
Where Claude was the MOST reliable: Claude was most reliable when we were debugging problems using the actual tool output. One example was when make memcheck failed immediately after make asan, reporting that the ASan runtime was not first in the library list. Rather than assuming there was a memory-management bug in my red-black tree, Claude correctly identified that Make had reused an ASan executable beause the source files did not change. It suggested running make clean && make memcheck, which solved the issue and had a clean Valgrind report. When the same problem reappeared, Claude caught it immediately. This showed me that Claude was very useful when it was given concrete error messages and test goals to reason through, even though its workaround did not permanently fix the underlying Makefile issue. 

Where Claude was the LEAST reliable: While I was determining what work was still required wihtout checking the assignment spec directly. I asked it to identify outsanding tasks, and it found 3 final open items. I challenged them as I realized certain ones such as pool.c or fault_alloc were not part of this assignment. And a test Claude believed to be missing was not required. If I accepted the first response, I would have spent a significant amount of time on unnecessary items. This showed me that Claude's answers even when told to check specifically, must be double checked against constraints and must find what is reasonable rather than what appears to be missing. 

A bug Claude introduced: Claude originally wrote two tests labeled as red-sibling deletion cases, but the insertion did not actually produce red siblings, rather, it would creat a different red-black-tree configuration, meaning the tests were not executing the proprer deletion-fixup case. 

I did not initially notice the wrong coloring myself. But before approving the implemetation plan I asked Claude to trace how each test got to its designated deletion case. This prompted Claude to compile and run an instrumented version of the actual implementation, finding tha tits hand-simulated tree colors were incorrect. We then proceeded to replace the two sequences with empirically verified ones and documented the findings.

This showed me that verification is a non-negotionable rather than assuming test-cases that simply look correct. A test can pass while still failing to execute the statements it supposedly covers, and the verification requirement I adopted allowed us to find the mistake before more progress had happened.

What surprised me the most as a C newcomer was how pointers worked, while they look simple given they're literally just a -> or a *. It took a while to learn how they really work. I also liked how the syntax isn't too different from Java. I didn't know how important it was nor how memory management worked. I had to understand that it wasn't as easy as just calling free(). I had to find out how to properly have a single stage of freeing in order to avoid a double free or use-after-free. I also had to find out that sometimes it would be simple, such as freely removing red node children.

Committed `21a44be`. Here's what's actually left, checked against the repo rather than from memory.

## Code

**Mutation 2 — one slice left.** `rb_create_pooled` is declared in the frozen header and appears nowhere in `src/` except comments. That's the integration slice: node storage from the pool, keys still through `rb_malloc` (variable length), and `rb_destroy` still walking every node to release keys and values *before* the pool goes away — the pool reclaims node storage, not the heap nodes point at. Then re-running the whole HW1 + M1 battery, fault sweep included, over the pooled build.

**Mutation 3 — not started.** `src/rbtree.c:298` still calls `foreach_inorder`, so `rb_foreach` is recursive, while the frozen header says "Mutation 3: O(1) auxiliary space, no recursion." `rb_destroy` already satisfies it (the Reach, from HW1). So: Morris traversal or parent-pointer threading for `rb_foreach`, plus the large-case harness — the Makefile has no million-node target, and NOTES.md already records the constraint (large case under asan, smaller under valgrind, and *say so in REFLECTION.md* rather than quietly shrinking it). One thing I'd want to check against the spec rather than guess: `rb_validate` recurses too (`validate_walk`), and the header annotates only `rb_foreach`/`rb_destroy` — so whether the 64 KB-stack threshold binds `rb_validate` is a question for §9, not something I should assume either way.

**Mutation 4 — not started.** `rb_snapshot`, O(1) copy-on-write. CLAUDE.md is explicit that reusing the Reach technique here is a from-scratch design question, not a copy-paste of `rb_destroy`.

## Process deliverables

- **DEVLOG**: slices B and C are both unlogged. Slice C in particular has material worth keeping — two mutants (`free_count++` dropped, free-head not advanced) that no assertion in the suite catches, only the debug walk.
- **PROMPTLOG**: 7 episodes, none covering tonight. It also closes with a standing note, "no rejected or oversized diff," which is one of the four required episode types. There's now real material for the gap: you cut `pool_destroy(NULL)`-safety and NULL-tolerant `pool_stats` outputs from my slice-A proposal, and rejected unconditional poisoning in favour of a debug gate. The two escaped mutants (b4's `stride`/`obj_size` blindness, c2 passing on recycled `0xDD` heap bytes) are good adversarial-review material too.
- **REFLECTION.md**: 11 lines, entirely HW1 — nothing on the pool, and the `kmem_cache`/Solaris comparison paragraph DEVLOG has been carrying as owed since Oct 6 is still owed.
- **Transcripts — the time-sensitive one.** `transcripts/` holds the HW1 `.jsonl` files plus `HW2-transcripts.zip`, which covers three sessions dated **Oct 2–3 only**. The Oct 6, 7 and 8 sessions (geometry, slice A, slices B and C) are not in the repo. Meanwhile the live project directory holds four files, the oldest dated **Sep 11** and **Sep 25** — and transcripts auto-purge after 30 days, so the Sep 11 one is around three days from expiring. Also worth a second thought: the spec says the actual `.jsonl` files "copied in as-is," and a zip may or may not satisfy a grader reading that literally.

Commit count is not a concern — 31 `M<n>:` commits.

## Small open item

`make memcheck` after `make asan` silently runs the ASan binaries under valgrind and reports `0 allocs, 0 frees`. It bit me in slices A and C. A `memcheck: clean all` dependency fixes it; I've left it alone twice because you ruled out unrelated Makefile changes, but it's a false-green risk rather than a style nit.

My suggestion for sequencing: copy the transcripts out first since that's the only item with a deadline, then `rb_create_pooled` to finish M2 before switching contexts. Say which and I'll propose it.
